description: Make product packshot photos that show the front, back, and buttons of your item on a clean backdrop. Upload one photo per side and build your gallery today.
h1: Product Packshot Photos for Multiple Views of Your Item
lead: Product packshot photos start with a separate source photo for each side you want to show. Build a square set around the front, back, top, or base views buyers need in your gallery. Mention the view a buyer needs, such as rear ports or a base label, so each run has one clear job and the gallery remains easy to scan.
intro: A packshot is a clean photo of the product alone, with nothing to pull the eye away from it. In the example, a light gray fabric-covered wireless speaker with a woven wrist strap sits on a soft gray backdrop, its control buttons facing the camera.

Online shoppers can't turn a product over in their hands, so they look for the back, the base, and the buttons in your gallery. Run this once for each side you photograph and keep the same backdrop words, and the views line up as a set on your Amazon or Shopify listing.
tip: Shoot each side straight on in daylight, and upload the back and base as separate photos so ports and labels come from your real product instead of a guess.

faq.q: Should I photograph each side separately?
faq.a: Yes. Give the back, base, and close details their own sharp source photos when shoppers need to see them. A separate source for each side keeps ports, controls, and labels tied to the real surface instead of asking the tool to invent a hidden view.

faq.q: Can one photo reveal a hidden port?
faq.a: Use a real photo of that side so the port and its placement come from your item. Keep the front hero first, then put the view that answers the most frequent question, such as connector type or closure, before less important angles.

Add the front first, then use side views to show controls, connectors, closures, or other product details. A clear JPG, PNG, or WebP is sufficient; use matching light and a stable camera distance so the set looks consistent.

faq.q: What file format and size should the source photos be?
faq.a: JPG, PNG, or Web Photos that clearly show the whole product work best. Shoot the front, back, and any port or button in similar light so the gallery reads as one set. Three or four views cover many small listings, but add a base or control view when it resolves a question buyers regularly ask.

faq.q: How many angle photos do I need?
faq.a: Three to four cover most listings: a front hero, a back view, and one or two detail angles. Start with the views shoppers ask about most.  Check the full item and its controls in the source before generating; hidden ports should come from a real view, not an invented angle.

faq.q: How many credits does each angle photo cost?
faq.a: Each generated angle photo costs 24 credits, and the cost appears before you run it. A failed job returns its credits to your balance.  Use one front hero, one rear or side view, and one detail view when the product has controls or connectors buyers need to inspect.

overview.h2: Build a Gallery That Lets Shoppers Turn the Product Over
overview.p: A single hero image cannot answer every question about a device. A matching set can show the charging port, control surface, hinge, back panel, and base in the order a shopper naturally inspects them. Start from real photos of the sides you want to publish, then use one visual description so the set feels like one shoot.

overview.h2: Use Each View for a Specific Decision
overview.p: Put the clearest front view first, then use the remaining frames for fit, connection, and construction details. This suits a speaker, lamp, charger, case, or boxed accessory when the product has distinct surfaces that can be photographed directly.

examples.lead: Separate views make small product features easier to see.

visual.overview: Show the front, rear, top, and base from separate photos of the real item so shoppers can inspect the parts they cannot turn over online. Keep the camera height, distance, backdrop, and shadow direction consistent across the set. A speaker can show its grille, controls, strap, ports, and feet; a charger can show its connector and rating panel. Use the front as the gallery lead, then put the view that answers the most common question next. Every generated angle still needs a check against the supplied product before it goes live. Keep reflections controlled on glossy electronics and leave enough margin around corners for a consistent crop. This approach helps sellers answer fit, connection, and construction questions with real views.
